(A) Fold’EM alternates structural inference with pose and class refinement. (B) Particle evidence is back-propagated into intermediate Pairformer states 𝐇 \mathbf{H} , filtering experimental updates through the remaining Pairformer blocks before AlphaFold3 diffusion. (C) For the integrin–BIIG2 Fab complex (PDB 9B9J ), AlphaFold3 predicts the individual components but places the Fab at the wrong binding site. (D) Ab initio Fold’EM recovers the bound complex and epitope from only 1,000 1{,}000 particles— 0.26 % 0.26\% of those used for the deposited reconstruction—with RMSD 2.49 ​ Å 2.49\,\text{\AA} , TM-score 0.956 0.956 , and FSC resolution 3.52 ​ Å 3.52\,\text{\AA} (deposited map: 2.6 ​ Å 2.6\,\text{\AA} ). We introduce Fold’EM , an inference-time framework that guides protein structure generative models directly using cryo-EM particle images. Rather than first reconstructing a three-dimensional density and subsequently building an atomic model into it, Fold’EM uses sequence-conditioned structural priors to infer atomic structures directly from sparse particle observations. We formulate structure determination as joint inference over the structural representation and particle-specific latent variables, including pose and conformational assignment (Figure 1 ). Particle vs. density guidance. We characterize when inference from individual particle images can be replaced by inference from a reconstructed density. For a homogeneous sample with known poses, we show that the two are equivalent only when density mismatch is measured under the experiment-induced metric defined by the imaging operators and noise model. The standard density-space L 2 L_{2} objective therefore does not, in general, reproduce the particle likelihood.

When poses or conformational assignments are uncertain, the distinction becomes more fundamental, as collapsing particles into a consensus density can discard particle-specific information required to infer these latent variables (Figure 3 ). This provides the statistical motivation for introducing structural priors directly at the particle level. Improved experimental guidance. Existing approaches condition AlphaFold on experimental data either by optimizing its terminal embedding before sampling ( Maddipatla et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026 ) , or by directly guiding the diffusion trajectory in coordinate space ( Maddipatla et al., 2025 ; Maddipatla et al., 2026b ; Raghu et al., 2026 ) . Fold’EM instead optimizes intermediate representations within the Pairformer module. Passing experimental updates through the remaining Pairformer blocks induces a sequence- and state-dependent geometry in the terminal conditioning space, constraining perturbations through transformations learned by the pretrained model. We find that this reparameterization substantially strengthens experimental guidance (Figure 3 ) and is a key enabling component of direct particle-level structure inference. Low-sample structure inference. We first evaluate Fold’EM in the known-pose setting, where it recovers accurate atomic structures on both experimental (Figure 4 ; Tables A3 – A4 ) and synthetic (Tables A5 – A6 ) datasets using fewer than 1 % 1\% of the particles used for conventional density reconstruction. Structures inferred directly from particle images reach comparable structural resolution to those obtained through density reconstruction, and on experimental homogeneous data from EMPIAR, as few as 0.1 % 0.1\% of the particles are sufficient to reach comparable Fourier shell correlation (FSC) and atomic RMSD. Heterogeneous results are shown in Figures 6 and 5 , Tables A15 – A16 and A19 – A20 .

In continuously heterogeneous systems, we further find that the organization of conformational states in particle space is reflected in the AlphaFold embedding space, indicating that experimentally observed conformational structure is preserved within the learned representation and allowing a continuous trajectory to be represented by a small number of optimized anchor states (Figure 9 ). Ab initio Fold’EM. We further propose ab initio Fold’EM, a framework for structure determination from cryo-EM particles with unknown poses and conformational states. The problem is formulated as a joint inference of the atomic structures, particle poses, and class assignments under the particle-level likelihood and sequence-conditioned structural prior. We solve this as a joint optimization problem by alternating between two stages: (i) structure inference given the current poses and class assignments , which uses particle-level guidance to optimize the atomic structures; (ii) pose and class inference given the inferred structures , which refines each particle’s pose and class assignment under the current structural ensemble. For low-sample heterogeneous data, we further introduce a RECOVAR-inspired residual-subspace estimator, B-RECOVAR, that provides more robust particle assignments and confidence estimates, which are used to prioritize reliable assignments during heterogeneous structure inference (Figure 7 , and Table A26 ). In experimental datasets with unknown poses, ab initio Fold’EM reaches comparable structural accuracy using approximately 3 % 3\% of the particles used in the deposited reconstruction (Figure 4 , Tables A9 – A10 ). In heterogeneous data, it resolves distinct conformational states using approximately 5 % 5\% of the particles (experimental: Figure 6 , Tables A17 – A18 ; synthetic: Tables A21 – A22 ).

Together, these results show that strong structural priors can substantially reduce the particle counts needed for atomic and conformational inference and suggest a route toward characterizing low-population states directly from cryo-EM particle images. 3 Methods Fold’EM jointly infers an ensemble of atomic structures and particle-specific nuisance variables directly from raw cryo-EM particle images. Each ensemble member is represented by an intermediate Pairformer state that conditions the AlphaFold3 diffusion model, and the nuisance variables of a particle are its pose and, in a heterogeneous sample, its discrete class. Fold’EM first places the particles in a common reference frame and, for heterogeneous data, assigns initial classes; it then alternates between updating the structural states given the particle images and refining the nuisance variables under the current ensemble. Reconstructed volumes, when used, serve only for initialization and class-specific frame alignment; structural guidance itself operates on individual particles. In what follows, we describe the ingredients of this solver of Equation 2 , schematically depicted in Figure 1 and summarized in Algorithm 1 . 3.1 Inputs, initialization, and reference frame Inputs. The inputs to Fold’EM are a collection of particle images and the molecular sequence specification 𝐚 \mathbf{a} of the target. We assume knowledge of the pixel/box size and CTF parameters from preprocessing; additionally, the particles are assumed to be centered. The sequence is the only structural input. AlphaFold3 constructs its MSA and unguided prediction from it, and no deposited atomic model or high-resolution experimental reconstruction is supplied. For heterogeneous data the number of classes n n is specified; for homogeneous data, n = 1 n=1 . Poses and class labels are provided only in the known-pose and known-class evaluations, in which the poses are those of the deposited consensus refinement. Pose estimation.

In the ab initio setting, poses are estimated in three stages: (i) VDAM, a variable-metric gradient descent algorithm with adaptive moments estimation ( Kimanius et al., 2021 ) , jointly estimates a coarse volume and particle poses from random initialization by marginalizing over poses; (ii) a consensus density is reconstructed from these poses by Wiener back-projection; and (iii) an AlphaFold3 prediction is docked into this density by L 1 L_{1} map guidance to define a structural reference frame. Since the cryo-EM likelihood is invariant to a global rigid transformation of the structure and the corresponding inverse transformation of the poses, the solution is defined only up to a global SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) transformation. We fix this gauge by expressing all particle poses relative to the docked structure before particle classification and structural inference. Particle embedding and classification. When class labels are unknown, we infer them directly from the particle images, without state-specific reference structures or atomic models. We consider cryoDRGN ( Zhong et al., 2021 ) , which embeds particles using a learned latent representation, and RECOVAR ( Gilles and Singer, 2025 ) , which embeds them by projection onto principal components of the estimated volume covariance. In the low-particle regime, however, experimental nuisance variation can be comparable to the structural differences of interest, and we find that these embeddings do not reliably separate classes. We therefore introduce B-RECOVAR, a bootstrapped residual-subspace estimator inspired by RECOVAR.

For the two-state case, it (i) fits class-deviation volumes to residuals from a consensus reconstruction, pooled through the current poses and restricted by a solvent mask; (ii) refines assignments by cross-validated comparison against per-class reconstructions; and (iii) combines the assignments from randomized subsamples and frequency bands using a label-free spectral meta-learner ( Parisi et al., 2014 ) . For more than two states, successive modes are extracted by deflation; for continuous heterogeneity, the same modes are interpreted as variability directions. The ensemble vote margin defines a per-particle confidence score, which is used to prioritize reliable assignments during structural inference. After classification, we reconstruct one auxiliary consensus volume per class, used only to establish its reference frame. We dock the reference structure into each volume as in the pose-estimation stage and re-synchronize particle poses to the corresponding class reference. The resulting classified particles, reference ensemble, and poses are then passed to structural inference. The full procedure is given in Algorithm 2 and Appendix D.4 , which also details its relation to RECOVAR. 3.2 Ensemble inference The inputs to structure inference are the particles, the reference structure, and the poses expressed with respect to it; for a heterogeneous sample, they are the classified particles, the ensemble of references, and the poses re-synchronized to their classes. Equation 2 couples the structural states 𝓗 \bm{\mathcal{H}} with the particle-specific nuisance variables 𝜼 \bm{\eta} , and we approximately optimize the two blocks by alternating coordinate ascent. Given the current nuisance estimates, we infer structures by an IT-Opt-style update ( Maddipatla et al., 2026a ) ; given the resulting structures, we refine the nuisance variables. Depending on the evaluation setting, known poses or classes are held fixed rather than updated.

Step 2: nuisance inference given structure. We next hold the structural ensemble 𝓧 ( r + 1 ) \bm{\mathcal{X}}^{(r+1)} fixed and update the nuisance variables as 𝜼 ( r + 1 ) = arg ⁡ max 𝜼 ​ [ log ⁡ p ⁡ ( 𝓨 ∣ 𝓧 ( r + 1 ) , 𝜼 ) + log ⁡ p ⁡ ( 𝜼 ) ] . \bm{\eta}^{(r+1)}=\arg\max_{\bm{\eta}}\left[\log p(\bm{\mathcal{Y}}\mid\bm{\mathcal{X}}^{(r+1)},\bm{\eta})+\log p(\bm{\eta})\right]. (6) In this work, the unknown nuisance variables are particle pose and structural class. Assuming their priors factorize across particles, the update can be performed independently for each particle as ( ϕ k ( r + 1 ) , c k ( r + 1 ) ) = arg ⁡ max ϕ , c ​ [ log ⁡ p ⁡ ( 𝐲 k ∣ 𝐗 c , ( r + 1 ) , ϕ ) + log ⁡ p ⁡ ( ϕ , c ) ] . (\bm{\phi}_{k}^{(r+1)},c_{k}^{(r+1)})=\arg\max_{\bm{\phi},c}\left[\log p(\mathbf{y}_{k}\mid\mathbf{X}^{c,(r+1)},\bm{\phi})+\log p(\bm{\phi},c)\right]. Pose refinement therefore aligns each particle against the currently inferred structures, while class refinement assigns it to the ensemble member that best explains its image. Poses remain expressed in the docked reference frame, fixing the otherwise arbitrary global SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) gauge. The updated nuisance variables are then returned to Equation 3 , and the two coordinate steps are alternated. This coupling is particularly important in the low-signal regime. Inaccurate poses or class assignments can produce misleading structural gradients, while an inaccurate structural model can in turn bias particle alignment and classification. If both coordinate steps were solved exactly for a deterministic objective, each iteration would be non-decreasing in Equation 2 and convergence would yield a coordinate-wise stationary solution.

In practice, the structural step uses stochastic diffusion samples, minibatches of particles, and finite gradient updates, so monotonic improvement is not guaranteed at every iteration. We therefore use the coordinate-ascent interpretation primarily as the organizing principle for joint structure and nuisance inference. 4 Experiments We evaluate Fold’EM on synthetic particles rendered from deposited structures and on experimental particle stacks from EMPIAR (Tables A2 and A1 ). Sections 4.1 and 4.2 test in isolation the two design choices of Sections 2 and 3 , namely guidance by the particles rather than by a reconstructed density, and optimization of the intermediate Pairformer state rather than of the terminal embedding or the atomic coordinates. Sections 4.3 and 4.4 evaluate structure determination for homogeneous samples and for two-state mixtures, in each case first with known poses, which tests structure inference alone, and then ab initio , with poses and classes inferred from the particles as described in Section 3.1 . In the known-pose setting the poses are those used to render the synthetic particles or, for experimental data, those of the deposited consensus refinement. Section 4.5 evaluates the label-free class assignment by B-RECOVAR that initializes the heterogeneous experiments, and Section 4.6 treats continuous heterogeneity. Unless stated otherwise, we report the C α \alpha RMSD and TM-score against the deposited model, and the resolution at which the Fourier shell correlation (FSC) against the deposited map crosses 0.143 0.143 (Appendix D.2.4 ); for synthetic data the deposited model is the ground truth from which the particles were rendered. The density-based baselines are RELION ( Zivanov et al., 2018 ) and cryoDRGN ( Zhong et al., 2021 ) with known poses, and RELION ab initio and cryoDRGN-AI ( Levy et al., 2025 ) without them (Appendix D.2 ).

We also report the unguided AlphaFold3 prediction, which represents the structure obtained without experimental conditioning and serves as a control for its effect. 4.1 Particle guidance vs. density guidance Figure 2: Guiding with the particles recovers the structure, whereas guiding with their reconstructed ESP fails. Experimental setup. We first ask whether guidance by the individual particles recovers more of the structure than guidance by the density reconstructed from them, at equal particle count. To evaluate this, we take the synthetic 8U4E assembly, the largest target in Table A2 ( 3,304 3{,}304 residues), and perform ab initio inference from 500 500 particles at SNR 0.005 0.005 . A consensus density is reconstructed from these particles at the estimated poses. Density guidance, the baseline, optimizes the same Pairformer state with the same particles, poses and optimizer as Fold’EM, but replaces the particle likelihood by a loss against this consensus density. The two settings therefore differ only in the data term. Results. At equal particle count, particle guidance recovers the assembly and density guidance does not. The unguided AlphaFold3 prediction misplaces the domains of 8U4E (C α \alpha RMSD 22.99 ​ Å 22.99\,\text{\AA} ). Density guidance reduces this only to 17.95 ​ Å 17.95\,\text{\AA} , whereas Fold’EM, guided by the same particles while refining their poses, reaches 6.88 ​ Å 6.88\,\text{\AA} with TM-score 0.809 0.809 (Table A12 ) and is the only one whose domains follow the envelope of the density (Figure 3 ).

As argued in Section 2 , a density loss reproduces the particle likelihood only for known poses and under the experiment-induced metric 𝐐 \mathbf{Q} , and with estimated poses the consensus density is not a sufficient statistic for the particles. At 500 500 particles the density is coarse and formed at uncertain poses; it serves to initialize the reference frame (Section 3.1 ) but cannot replace the particles as the data term. 4.2 Optimizing 𝓗 \bm{\mathcal{H}} vs. 𝓩 \bm{\mathcal{Z}} vs. coordinate-space guidance Experimental setup. We next ask whether optimizing the intermediate Pairformer state 𝓗 \bm{\mathcal{H}} gives stronger particle guidance than optimizing the terminal embedding 𝓩 \bm{\mathcal{Z}} or guiding the atomic coordinates directly. To evaluate this, we take synthetic 9UGB and 8U4B at SNR 0.005 0.005 with 250 250 or 1,000 1{,}000 particles and known poses, so that differences reflect the guidance mechanism rather than pose estimation. We compare Fold’EM with IT-Opt ( Maddipatla et al., 2026a ) , which optimizes 𝓩 \bm{\mathcal{Z}} under an isotropic prior (see also Li et al., 2026 ), and with coordinate-space guidance of the reverse diffusion process ( Maddipatla et al., 2026b ) . The three schemes use the same particle likelihood, poses and particle subsets, and differ only in the variable that the likelihood gradient updates. Results. Optimizing 𝓗 \bm{\mathcal{H}} gives the strongest guidance of the three. All three schemes correct the AlphaFold3 prediction of 9UGB , and Fold’EM attains the lowest C α \alpha RMSD, highest TM-score and finest FSC resolution. On the larger 8U4B assembly, Fold’EM recovers the deposited structure, whereas IT-Opt and coordinate-space guidance degrade the initial prediction (Figure 3 ). The particles thus correct the relative arrangement of the predicted components and reveal the epitope, although the interface variable loops of BIIG2 are not recovered with atomic accuracy.

Finally, we ask whether a continuous conformational trajectory can be represented by a small number of optimized Pairformer states and their interpolation.

To evaluate this, we take the IgG-1D dataset of CryoBench ( Jeon et al., 2024 ) , which consists of 100 100 ground-truth atomic models, generated from PDB entry 1HZH by rotating one Fab domain about the hinge through a closed 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} trajectory, and 25,000 25{,}000 synthetic particles at SNR 0.01 0.01 , 250 250 per state, with ground-truth poses and per-particle CTFs. We embed each particle in three label-free conformational coordinates, namely the latent of a cryoDRGN VAE trained on the stack, the leading principal components of RECOVAR, and the residual-subspace embedding of B-RECOVAR (Appendix D.4 ). Each coordinate defines one arm of the experiment, and the arms differ only in the coordinate used to select the particles of each state. In each arm, we fix eight anchor conformations at equispaced positions along the ring and, for each anchor, optimize one structure against the 250 250 particles nearest to it in the conformational coordinate of that arm. This yields eight Pairformer states 𝐇 1 , … , 𝐇 8 \mathbf{H}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{H}_{8} , optimized independently against disjoint particle sets, with no term coupling them. An intermediate conformation at position α \alpha along the ring is obtained as the convex combination 𝐇 ⁡ ( α ) = ∑ k c k ​ ( α ) ​ 𝐇 k \mathbf{H}(\alpha)=\sum_{k}c_{k}(\alpha)\,\mathbf{H}_{k} of the two neighbouring anchors, with piecewise-linear coefficients c k c_{k} . For each of the 100 100 ground-truth states we decode 𝐇 ⁡ ( α ) \mathbf{H}(\alpha) through a full reverse-diffusion trajectory, with a brief coordinate-space refinement against the 250 250 particles that the same coordinate places nearest to that state, and relax the result (Appendix D.2.3 ). The comparison is among the three coordinates, and between the interpolated structures and the anchors, rather than against a density-based baseline.

Each structure is scored by the TM-score against the ground-truth model of its state and by the Fourier NCC between the rendered structure and the particles of that state, expressed as a fraction of the NCC of the ground-truth model against the same particles. Results. Eight anchors suffice to represent the trajectory. Over the full ring, the 100 100 structures of the B-RECOVAR arm, all decoded from interpolated states, attain a median NCC of 92 % 92\% of the ground-truth value and a median TM-score of 0.93 0.93 , comparable to the eight anchors themselves ( 89 % 89\% and 0.91 0.91 ). The cryoDRGN coordinate reaches 85 % 85\% and 0.89 0.89 , and the RECOVAR coordinate 90 % 90\% and 0.92 0.92 (Figure 9 ). The leading principal components of the optimized Pairformer states preserve the ordering in hinge angle for all three coordinates (Figure 9 ), although the anchors are optimized independently and nothing in the objective couples them. Table A25 reports the stereochemical quality of the anchors and of the interpolated structures. The conformational organization of the particles is therefore mirrored in the AlphaFold representation, and a continuous trajectory can be represented by a small number of experimentally optimized states. 6 Conclusion We introduced Fold’EM, an inference-time framework that infers atomic structures directly from cryo-EM particle images by guiding AlphaFold3 with particle-level evidence, bypassing density reconstruction and model building. We showed that density fitting reproduces the particle likelihood only under the experiment-induced metric and that, under pose or class uncertainty, a consensus density need not be a sufficient statistic; and that optimizing intermediate rather than terminal Pairformer states induces a learned geometry that substantially strengthens guidance.

Fold’EM recovers accurate structures from fewer than 1 % 1\% of the particles used by conventional reconstruction with known poses, roughly 3 % 3\% ab initio , and roughly 5 % 5\% for heterogeneous samples, recovering features missed by the unguided prediction, such as the Integrin α 5 ​ β 1 \alpha_{5}\beta_{1} –BIIG2 binding site and the distorted DNA of UvrA. Conformational organization in particle space is also reflected in the AlphaFold representation, so that continuous motions can be represented by a few anchor states. Together, these results suggest a shorter route to structure determination in which the prior supplies what is already known and the experiment determines what it does not: assembly, conformation, and interaction geometry. Limitations. Fold’EM is not yet an end-to-end replacement for the cryo-EM pipeline: inputs are curated particle collections with known CTF parameters, and ab initio inference relies on accurate pose estimates for initialization. Components absent from the model, such as glycans, ligands or flexible regions, are treated as unexplained signal, and fine local details, such as interface loops, remain harder to recover than global assemblies and major conformational changes. Uncurated particles, unmodelled density, better pose initialization, and finer local refinement are natural directions for future work. D.3.2 Noise model and likelihood function The fundamental electron-detection noise is shot noise and is therefore Poisson at the level of individual electron counts. The particle images used for reconstruction, however, are processed rather than raw counting measurements: detector response, frame integration, motion correction, dose weighting, gain correction, background subtraction, normalization, and other sources of experimental uncertainty make a simple pixelwise Poisson model inappropriate for the resulting images. As is standard in likelihood-based single-particle cryo-EM reconstruction [ Scheres, 2012 ] , we therefore model the residual image noise as additive Gaussian noise, allowing its variance to depend on spatial frequency. Specifically, let 𝐲 c \mathbf{y}_{c} denote a candidate noiseless particle image and assume additive Gaussian noise in the Fourier domain, 𝐲 ^ = 𝐲 ^ c + 𝐍 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{y}}=\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{c}+\widehat{\mathbf{N}} . We follow the community practice and model each Fourier coefficient of 𝐍 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{N}} as an independent zero-mean complex Gaussian with frequency-dependent variance σ 2 ​ ( 𝝎 ) \sigma^{2}(\bm{\omega}) .

The corresponding noise log-likelihood is, up to an additive constant, log p ( 𝐲 ∣ 𝐲 c ) = − 1 2 ∑ 𝝎 ∈ Ω | 𝐲 ^ ​ ( 𝝎 ) − 𝐲 ^ c ​ ( 𝝎 ) | 2 σ 2 ​ ( 𝝎 ) . \log p(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{y}_{c})=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Omega}\frac{\left|\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\bm{\omega})-\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{c}(\bm{\omega})\right|^{2}}{\sigma^{2}(\bm{\omega})}. (13) The Gaussian model should be understood as an effective likelihood for processed cryo-EM particle images rather than as a model of the underlying electron-arrival process. In practice, we do not optimize this Gaussian log-likelihood directly. Instead, we use a band-limited normalized correlation between the observed and simulated particle images in Fourier space, ℒ corr ​ ( 𝐲 , 𝐲 c ) = Re ⁡ [ ∑ 𝝎 ∈ Ω 𝐲 ^ ​ ( 𝝎 ) ​ 𝐲 ^ c ​ ( 𝝎 ) ∗ ] ∑ 𝝎 ∈ Ω | 𝐲 ^ ​ ( 𝝎 ) | 2 ​ ∑ 𝝎 ∈ Ω | 𝐲 ^ c ​ ( 𝝎 ) | 2 + ϵ , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{corr}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}_{c})=\frac{\operatorname{Re}\!\left[\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Omega}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\bm{\omega})\,{\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{c}(\bm{\omega})}^{\ast}\right]}{\sqrt{\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Omega}|\widehat{\mathbf{y}}(\bm{\omega})|^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{\bm{\omega}\in\Omega}|\widehat{\mathbf{y}}_{c}(\bm{\omega})|^{2}}+\epsilon}, where Ω = { 𝝎 : k min ≤ ‖ 𝝎 ‖ 2 < k max + 1 } \Omega=\{\bm{\omega}:k_{\min}\leq\|\bm{\omega}\|_{2}<k_{\max}+1\} is the frequency band used for guidance and ϵ \epsilon is a small numerical stabilizer. Maximizing this objective is equivalent to minimizing squared error between the observed and simulated Fourier images after normalizing both to unit norm. It can therefore be viewed as a scale-invariant surrogate for the Gaussian image log-likelihood. We use this surrogate because the overall amplitude and contrast of experimental cryo-EM particles can vary for reasons that are not informative about molecular structure.

The normalization removes sensitivity to such global scale differences and makes the guidance depend primarily on agreement in the spatial-frequency content and phase structure of the particle. Restricting the comparison to Ω \Omega further excludes very low frequencies dominated by background and normalization effects, as well as high frequencies with little reliable signal. Compared with the full Gaussian likelihood, this objective discards explicit frequency-dependent noise weighting in favor of a simpler and empirically more robust similarity measure for inference-time optimization.
